title: Universal In-Plane Confined Growth of Mesoporous Metal–Organic Framework Crystalline Heterostructures
abstract: Abstract Constructing mesoporous MOF heterostructures on conductive two-dimensional hosts remains challenging because interfacial contact and pore accessibility are rarely optimized simultaneously. Herein, we report a universal in-plane confined growth strategy for mesoporous UiO-66-NH2/MXene heterostructures featuring continuous interfacial contact and vertically accessible mesochannels. In contrast to conventional particle-on-sheet hybrids, the resulting architecture enables improved electrolyte penetration, shortened Zn2+ transport pathways, and efficient interfacial electron transfer. By regulating micellar assembly at the interface, an optimal mesostructural regime is identified in which ion accessibility and structural confinement are best balanced. Consequently, the optimized heterostructure delivers a high energy density of 163.9 Wh kg–1, excellent rate capability (∼68% retention over a 50-fold current increase), and ∼100% capacity retention over 50,000 cycles. Kinetic analyses and ex situ studies further show that the interfacial mesoporous architecture suppresses diffusion limitations and preserves structural integrity during Zn2+ storage. Moreover, the assembly concept shows transferability across substrates of different dimensionalities, highlighting its broader utility for constructing mesoporous crystalline heterostructures. This work provides an effective route to mesoporous MOF heterostructures and a generalizable design principle for hybrid crystalline electrodes.

title: Review and Outlook on Biomass-Derived Carbon Materials and Their Functional Composites with 2D Materials for Sustainable Energy Storage Applications
abstract: Abstract The synergistic integration of sustainable biomass-derived carbon frameworks with highly conductive two-dimensional MXenes represents a promising frontier for bridging the energy–power gap in electrochemical energy-storage systems. This Review highlights the critical role of MXenes, transition-metal dichalcogenides (TMDs), and metal–organic frameworks (MOFs), along with their composites with biomass-derived activated carbon, in designing advanced electrodes for energy storage systems. Biomass-derived carbons offer renewable, low-cost, and hierarchically porous structures that facilitate efficient ion transport, while MXenes provide exceptional electrical conductivity and surface functionality. Meanwhile, MOFs and TMDs introduce tunable porosity and abundant redox-active sites, enabling enhanced pseudocapacitive and Faradaic charge storage. A central focus of this Review is the influence of synthesis strategies on structural evolution and electrochemical performance. Various synthesis approaches are critically discussed to demonstrate how they can tailor three-dimensional architectures, interfacial interactions, and pore distribution, thereby directly influencing key performance metrics, such as specific capacitance, energy density, rate capability, and cycling stability. In addition, the Review comprehensively examines essential characterization techniques and practical performance parameters, including scalability, oxidation stability, and electrolyte compatibility, providing insights into the realistic evaluation of device performance. Finally, future research directions are outlined with an emphasis on green and scalable synthesis routes, flexible and wearable device integration, and the development of electrically efficient and structurally robust architectures. This Review provides a comprehensive framework for the design of next-generation hybrid materials, paving the way for high-performance, sustainable, and commercially viable energy storage technologies.

title: Role of Intermolecular Association in Monolayer-Level Assembly and Morphogenesis of Conjugated Polymers at the Air–Water Interface
abstract: Abstract How molecular architecture is translated through intermolecular association into film structure and mechanical behavior remains a central question in conjugated-polymer self-assembly. Here, we compare two luminescent polymers with distinct backbone and side-chain structures: poly(9,9-di-n-octylfluorenyl-2,7-diyl) (PFO) and poly(2,5-di(3′,7′-dimethyloctyl)phenylene-1,4-ethynylene) (PPE). Langmuir–Blodgett processing provides a controlled two-dimensional environment at the air–water interface, while the intrinsic fluorescence of both polymers allows interfacial organization to be followed from the earliest stages of spreading. PFO rapidly forms discrete domains. PPE instead develops a laterally interconnected network. Molecular dynamics simulations relate these morphologies to different modes of intermolecular association. In PFO, fluorene units associate more locally, favoring compact aggregation. PPE instead forms more spatially distributed contacts along the phenylene–ethynylene backbone. This distinction persists during mechanical deformation. Compression brings pre-existing PFO domains into contact, but decompression rapidly fragments the film. PPE remains laterally connected and undergoes extensive expansion. Deformation is accommodated predominantly through the ethynylene linkages of the conjugated backbone. Beyond the monolayer stability limit, both polymers develop anisotropic semicrystalline structures. PFO forms isolated needle-like domains, whereas PPE develops an interconnected fibrillar network. The results thus establish a hierarchical link between local intermolecular association and the subsequent evolution of monolayer structure and mechanical behavior. This relationship remains reflected in the ordered structures formed after monolayer collapse and provides a basis for designing ultrathin conjugated-polymer films with controlled lateral connectivity and anisotropic organization.

title: Hydrogen-Bonded Organic Framework-Confined Carbon Dots toward Efficient Red Room-Temperature Phosphorescence via Resonance Energy Transfer
abstract: Abstract Room-temperature phosphorescence (RTP) materials are promising for information encryption and anticounterfeiting. However, realizing long-wavelength RTP of carbon dots (CDs) is challenging owing to unstable triplet states and strong nonradiative decay. Herein, we construct a hydrogen-bonded organic framework (HOF) through molecular self-assembly and realize the in situ generation of CDs within the HOF matrix. By further incorporating Rhodamine B (RhB) into the HOF, a donor–acceptor resonance energy transfer (RET) system is established, enabling efficient red RTP emission. In this system, the HOF matrix provides a confined environment for the CDs and RhB. Meanwhile, the hydrogen-bonded network restricts excited-state molecular motions and suppresses nonradiative relaxation. The optimized CDs-RhB@HOF composite exhibits outstanding red phosphorescence centered at 600 nm, achieving a high PLQY of 34.20% (versus 0.71% for CDs@HOF) and a prolonged lifetime of 458 ms. The composite material has been successfully applied to multilevel anticounterfeiting encryption.

title: Dichlorobenzodithiophene‐4‐8‐dione Derived Polymer Donor Enables Efficient Thin‐Film/Thick‐Film Organic Solar Cells
abstract: ABSTRACT Polymer donors with electron‐withdrawing benzodithiophene‐4‐8‐dione (BDD) unit play an important role in improving power‐conversion‐efficiency (PCE) of organic solar cells (OSCs), although these achievements rely on high‐cost electron‐donating fluorinated thienyl‐benzodithiophene (BDTT) moiety. Herein, a dichlorobenzodithiophene‐4‐8‐dione (BDD2Cl) unit is developed to design fluorine‐free BDTT‐ alt ‐BDD2Cl‐structured cost‐effective polymer donor (PBDTT‐BDD2Cl). Compared to its halogen‐free BDTT‐ alt ‐BDD‐structured control (PBDB‐T), PBDTT‐BDD2Cl shows deep‐shifted energy levels, improved solubility, crystallinity, and packing, tending to suppress energy loss, manipulate film‐forming kinetics, and improve charge transport properties. Accordingly, the PBDTT‐BDD2Cl:L8‐BO device demonstrates dramatically higher photovoltage (0.947 V) and lower non‐radiative energy loss (0.182 eV) and compared to the PBDB‐T:L8‐BO device (0.735 and 0.369 eV), while it achieves decreased PCE. When incorporating it into D18:L8‐BO host, ternary D18:PBDTT‐BDD2Cl:L8‐BO shows optimized donor/acceptor miscibility, delayed material nucleation, and prolonged molecular ordered packing duration, leading to boosted charge dynamics and favorable morphology. Thereby, thin‐film (100 nm) OSC achieves a superior PCE (21.1%, certified as 20.6%, ranking among the highest values) than the D18:PBDB‐T:L8‐BO control (19.3%), while its thick‐film (500 nm) device also obtains a top‐high PCE (17.3%) among these reported thick‐films (≥500 nm). This work highlights that BDD2Cl is an ideal candidate for developing cost‐effective polymer donors toward efficient thin‐film/thick‐film OSCs.

title: Versatile Interfacial Engineering of Core–Shell Mesoporous Nanomaterials: Programmable Assembly, Functional Integration, and Diverse Applications
abstract: Abstract Integrating diverse building blocks into functional materials with tailored architectures and properties has emerged as an efficient strategy to address the demands of multifunctional applications, and core–shell mesoporous materials (CSMMs) enable the modular integration of functional components and the structural optimization of mass transfer. Enabled by multi-interface nanoassembly strategies, diverse CSMMs have been engineered and sparked intense interdisciplinary interest owing to their distinctive features, including multicomponent synergistic effects, interfacial coupling effects, and rationally designed heterogeneous architectures. Herein, this review systematically introduces the concept of “micellar coating chemistry” and summarizes current assembly strategies for the tailored synthesis of CSMMs. The rational design of structure (e.g. surface roughness, cavity, pore size, and porosity) and composition (e.g. magnetic-, noble metal-, silica-, polymer-, and carbon-based components) are highlighted. Furthermore, functionality integration (e.g. nanoparticle loading, hybridization, and surface functionalization) is also evaluated and summarized, and the diverse applications of these materials in hot fields, such as catalysis, gas sensing, environmental remediation, biomedicine, energy storage and conversion, are critically assessed and compared. This review outlines future research opportunities and challenges, and establishes a conceptual foundation for the rational design, scalable synthesis, and versatile interdisciplinary applications of CSMMs.

title: Joule Heating Induced Structural Evolution of Ordered Mesoporous Mg-Al Spinel-Related Oxides
abstract: Coupling block copolymer self-assembly with ultrafast Joule heating enables second-scale crystallization of ordered mesoporous oxides while preserving long-range mesoscopic order. Using this strategy, we synthesize long-range ordered mesoporous magnesium-aluminum oxide frameworks at low magnesium contents exhibiting defect spinel-related nanocrystalline structures. Ex situ isothermal holds at 1000 to 1155 °C reveal rapid crystallite enlargement followed by a plateau in apparent crystallite size. In pure γ-alumina, this early saturation, together with retention of the ordered mesostructure, is consistent with geometrically constrained crystallite growth. Magnesium incorporation enables further crystallite enlargement before saturation, yielding larger defect-spinel-related domains while retaining long-range mesoscopic order. We further demonstrate the incorporation of in situ crystallized platinum nanoparticles within the ordered magnesium-aluminum oxide framework and their activity for methylcyclohexane dehydrogenation at 350 °C. These results demonstrate that ultrafast Joule heating can access distinct crystallization trajectories in compositionally modified mesoporous oxides that are precluded by mesostructural collapse during conventional furnace heating.

title: Porous Framework Assembly Creates Functional Tertiary Folds in Small Peptides
abstract: Abstract There is significant interest in recreating the protein tertiary structure in simpler systems, which can enable the precise and modular organization of multiple functional groups for enhancing molecular recognition and catalysis. Small peptides are minimalist analogs of proteins; however, their limited size highly disfavors folding into tertiary structures, especially those that also possess open binding sites needed for function. Here, we report that 3-dimensional self-assembly into a porous crystalline framework overcomes this limitation, producing modular tertiary structures in peptides shorter than 20 amino acids with tunable binding sites. As shown by X-ray crystallography, this framework-mediated folding tolerates many sequences with a broad range of functional groups, and it generates precise confined environments that are dynamic and mutationally robust. Thus, these pores can be programmed to selectively bind complex molecular guests such as nucleotides and perfluoroalkyl substances through the cooperative engagement of up to 10 distinct residues. These results demonstrate that a well-defined tertiary structure can exist in very short peptides and can impart tunable protein-like function to synthetic porous materials.

title: Charge-Transfer Engineering Controls Excited-State Dynamics and Supramolecular Assembly in Luminescent Au(I) Complexes
abstract: Abstract Coupling excited-state control with supramolecular self-assembly within a single molecular design remains a central challenge in luminescent materials chemistry. Here, we explore charge-transfer (CT) engineering as a strategy to address both features in a family of luminescent Au(I) bisphosphine complexes. Homoleptic derivatives bearing pyrene, phenanthrene, or triphenylene chromophores were compared with a heteroleptic pyrene/phenanthrene complex designed to promote interchromophoric electronic communication. The homoleptic complexes display predominantly room-temperature fluorescence, with increasing phosphorescence contributions associated with progressive metal perturbation of the excited states. In the heteroleptic complex, the combination of electronically differentiated chromophores enables access to a T2-mediated pathway that promotes room-temperature pyrene phosphorescence, as supported by solvent-dependent photophysical measurements and theoretical calculations. Addition of [Au(CN)2]− enhances fluorescence in all cases, with a 6-fold increase for the heteroleptic complex, and promotes its organization into extended luminescent wires driven by a combination of C–H···N≡C hydrogen bonding and π···π stacking interactions. These results show how chromophore differentiation within an Au(I) coordination scaffold can couple excited-state modulation with supramolecular organization, providing a design strategy for responsive luminescent assemblies.

title: Synergistic Dual-Fuel-Driven Dissipative (Opto-)Electronic Crystals: Unraveling Spatiotemporal Multifunctionality Beyond Equilibrium
abstract: Abstract Living systems sustain complex far-from-equilibrium structures through the continuous consumption of high-energy chemical fuels, a phenomenon known as dissipative self-assembly (DSA). While DSA has enabled the design of adaptive amorphous materials driven by a single fuel source, the construction of dissipative (opto-)electronic crystals utilizing different fuel inputs acting simultaneously remains a significant challenge. Here, we report a strategy for constructing out-of-equilibrium (opto-)electronic crystals driven by synergetic dual-fuel inputs (chemical and light). Using a bio-organic NG building block, chemical fuel consumption induces a transient condensation reaction that orchestrates successive hydration states of DSA, including colloidal particles and the formation of chiral crystals. Remarkably, the resulting dissipative crystals exhibit light-triggered transient generation of radical anions, providing an additional level of spatiotemporal regulation. Molecular dynamics simulations reveal the atomistic assembly features underlying the various states of the DSA process. Notably, this dual-fuel DSA platform endows the materials with spatiotemporally programmable multifunctionality, enabling self-erasable writing, Boolean-logic-based out-of-equilibrium patterning, and dissipative (opto-)electronic device properties. These findings establish a route toward life-like programmable molecular materials with adaptive responses and autonomous information-processing capabilities, offering new opportunities for smart materials and sustainable (opto-)electronic technologies.

title: Over 95% Optical Reflectance From Structurally Modulated All‐Biopolymer Multilayers
abstract: ABSTRACT Sustainable photonics aims to replace conventional optical materials with environmentally benign alternatives, yet its development is fundamentally constrained by the narrow intrinsic refractive‐index variability of biopolymers. Here we show that a dense–porous periodic architecture yields nearly perfect optical reflection using only polysaccharides. By exploiting the difference in skeletal rigidity between amorphous pectin and crystalline cellulose nanofibers (CNFs), we form alternating dense, high‐refractive‐index pectin layers and porous, low‐refractive‐index CNF layers through a combination of electrodeposition with solvent exchange. This dense–porous periodic architecture yields reflectivities exceeding 97% in the visible range and 95% in the near‐infrared—a range unprecedented for biopolymer‐based optical materials. Moreover, the strategy is simple, scalable, and highly versatile, enabling free spectral design across the visible and near‐infrared regions, broadband metallic‐like reflection, and planar patterning within a single fabrication process. Combined with the low thermal conductivity arising from porous layers and the coexistence of visible transparency and near‐infrared reflection, the resulting films show potential as transparent thermal‐management materials. This work establishes a new materials design principle for biodegradable, polysaccharide‐based photonic systems and advances the field of sustainable photonics.

title: Suprasilica Nanosieves for Selective Capture of Aromatics Over Cyclic Aliphatics in Hydrocarbon Feedstocks
abstract: ABSTRACT Separating aromatic from cyclic aliphatic hydrocarbons remains a major challenge, as conventional distillation is both energy‐intensive and poorly selective. Here, we report supramolecular silica nanosieves (suprasilica) that integrate organic molecular recognition sites directly into robust inorganic matrices. A hexasila‐ureido‐trianglamine (Δ‐Si 6 ) is co‐condensed within the silica matrix through a self‐assembly sol–gel approach at controlled loadings to produce suprasilica sieves ( Δ‐SiN x ). In vapor sorption, Δ‐SiN x reject cyclic aliphatic hydrocarbons while displaying high aromatic uptake, achieving benchmark ideal selectivity for benzene over cyclohexane (23.5, uptake 9.4 mmol g − 1 ) on Δ‐SiN20 and for toluene over methylcyclohexane (6.3, uptake 6.3 mmol g − 1 ) on Δ‐SiN10 . The selectivity was further confirmed by Dynamic Column Breakthrough experiments, which demonstrated efficient separation under dynamic conditions. Importantly, the Δ‐SiN x retain their molecular discrimination in the binary liquid phase, showing strong preferential uptake while preserving aromatic selectivity in neat naphtha and in diluted crude oil. Metadynamics simulations indicate that the selectivity is kinetic in origin, benzene passing the macrocyclic apertures with a modest barrier while cyclohexane is excluded. These suprasilica nanosieves deliver benchmark separation performance and provide a scalable, energy‐efficient strategy for hydrocarbon purification.

title: Hierarchical Engineering of Atomically Precise Gold Nanoclusters from Alloying to Cluster-Assembled Frameworks
abstract: Abstract Atomically precise gold nanoclusters (Au NCs) provide molecular-level platforms for understanding how atomic structure influences catalytic, photophysical, chiral, and electronic properties. Although alloying, ligand/interface engineering, and nanocluster assembly have each emerged as powerful approaches for tailoring Au NC function, they are often considered as separate design strategies. In this perspective, we organize recent advances in Au NC design across three interconnected levels of structural control: core alloying, ligand/interface engineering, and cluster-assembled materials. We discuss how alloying modifies the intrinsic electronic structure of the NC core, how ligand and interface engineering regulate the expression of these properties through electronic and structural control, and how coordination-mediated assembly organizes individual NCs into aggregates, superstructures, and crystalline frameworks with collective photophysical and electronic properties. By connecting these design strategies, this perspective provides a hierarchical view of Au NC design that links molecular precision to materials-level functionality and highlights opportunities for catalysis, sensing, optoelectronics, and nanoelectronics.

title: Guest Transition Metals in Host Keplerate Nanocapsules as Supramolecular Inorganic Functional Mimics of Monooxygenase Enzymes
abstract: ABSTRACT Advanced design of supramolecules can mimic enzyme complexes. Methane monooxygenases have several subparts, hydroxylases active for alkane oxidation, and complexes and channels that regulate electron, proton, substrate, and product access to the active site. The replication of a hydroxylase active site with inclusion of regulatory functionalities within a porous Keplerate nanocapsule host was undertaken. A Cu active site guest within a Keplerate cavity was prepared by an assembly reaction using a histidine surrogate as binding site for Cu II . The guest–host assembly enables transfer of protons and electrons and enables substrate and product diffusion to and from an active site into confined space. Characterization of the guest–host complex was by NMR, XPS, infrared, and Raman spectroscopies. Cyclic voltammetry was used to identify possible hydroxylase reactivity, followed by controlled potential electrolysis to verify hydrocarbon oxygenation. Substrate scope, optimal cathodic potential, and the number of metal sites needed were surveyed. Comparison of substrate reactivity revealed that their access to the active site was rate determining. Kinetics of a “dummy” substrate and product diffusion was measured by Guest Exchange Saturation Transfer 19 F NMR. These guest–host Keplerate nanocapsules represent an initial foray into the mimicking of a complicated metalloenzyme complex in an inorganic synthetic system.

title: Replacing CTAB with Renewable-Origin Surfactants for the Synthesis of Mesoporous 8YSZ: Structural Integrity, Functional Validation, and Sustainability Assessment
abstract: Abstract Cetyltrimethylammonium bromide (CTAB), a conventional structure-directing agent for mesoporous materials, is a petroleum-derived toxic compound whose removal requires energy-intensive multistep purification, increasing the environmental impact of the process. This study presents the sustainable synthesis of mesoporous 8 mol % yttria-stabilized zirconia (8YSZ) by replacing CTAB with glycerol (GLY) and glycerol monostearate (GMS), low-cost, renewable agents derived from the oleochemical industry. Raman spectroscopy, X-ray diffraction, electron microscopy, and N2 physisorption confirm the formation of fully cubic fluorite 8YSZ with mesoporous frameworks of interconnected nanocrystals, which exhibit appropriate macroporosity after high-temperature sintering. Ionic conductivity measurements, corrected for porosity, tortuosity, and constrictivity, demonstrate that scaffolds derived from renewable surfactants retain intrinsic oxygen-ion conduction equivalent to the CTAB reference and consistent with literature values for dense 8YSZ. A quantitative sustainability assessment shows that the renewable route reduces process mass intensity by up to 89% (from ∼710 to 78–81), energy intensity by 73% (from 3.87 to 1.03 kWh g–1), and production costs by up to 60%, while maintaining structural integrity in batches up to 10 g. These findings establish renewable surfactant substitution as a viable, scalable strategy for greener synthesis of functional porous ceramics, with direct relevance to electrochemical devices, catalyst substrates, and separation membranes.

title: Dual-Mode Exciton Coupling in Epitaxially Registered Organic–Inorganic 2D Heterocrystals
abstract: Abstract Two-dimensional (2D) heterocrystals comprising molecules and semiconductors can serve as an ideal platform for studying interfacial excitons and for future optoelectronic applications, yet the energy and charge flow across these atomically sharp interfaces remain unclear. In this work, we investigated PTCDA/MoS2 as a prototypical 2D organic–inorganic heterostructure and revealed dual-mode exciton coupling between the constituent crystals. Monolayer-resolved PTCDA molecular crystals were grown on monolayer MoS2 via physical vapor assembly, and their crystallographic details, including the stacking angle, were determined by electron diffraction. Upon the formation of the heterostructures, PTCDA’s photoluminescence was nearly completely quenched by efficient interfacial excited-state decay, whereas that of MoS2 increased markedly with PTCDA thickness. Using differential reflectance and photoluminescence excitation (PLE) spectroscopy, we found that the enhancement arises from two distinct contributions. One contribution, observed without direct PTCDA excitation, is consistent with ground-state charge transfer injecting holes into MoS2, which suppresses negative trion formation and enhances the radiative recombination of neutral excitons. The other, correlated with PTCDA absorption in the PLE response, supports resonance energy transfer, which diverts excitation energy from PTCDA to MoS2. Our findings help reconcile previously proposed mechanisms and show how molecular and MoS2 excitonic responses evolve with molecular thickness in a structurally defined heterocrystal.

title: Intermediate Phase Selectivity in ZSM-5 Zeolite Synthesis and Framework Aluminum Distribution
abstract: Abstract The current understanding of zeolite crystallization is still far from well understood. Herein, we show that the crystallization pathway of high-silica ZSM-5, one of the most industrially important zeolites, can be altered not only by the type of organic structure-directing agents (OSDAs) at a gel Si/Al ratio of 50 but also by the simultaneous use of Na+ and Cs+ ions as inorganic structure-directing agents (ISDAs). The use of the diquaternary OSDA 1,8-bis(N-methylpyrrolidinium)octane (1,8-MPO) instead of tetrapropylammonium (TPA), the most common OSDA for the synthesis of ZSM-5, in the presence of Na+ led to zeolite β as an intermediate phase; otherwise, no crystalline intermediate was observed. Also, the addition of a small amount of Cs+ ions (gel Cs/Na = 0.14) as a secondary ISDA to the 1,8-MPO-Na+ and TPA-Na+ systems gave small-pore zeolites bikitaite and analcime as an intermediate phase during synthesis, respectively. More importantly, we found that the framework Al distribution in the final product ZSM-5 could differ according to the in situ transformation pathway of intermediate phases, as well as to the type of OSDA used. This study provides a new strategy for directly controlling the intrazeolitic location of Brønsted acid sites, as well as the nucleation pathway in the synthesis of high-silica zeolites.

title: Guest-Programmed Adaptive Redistribution in Heteroleptic Metal–Organic Cages
abstract: Abstract Adaptive reconfiguration of complex supramolecular assemblies remains a fundamental challenge in synthetic chemistry, especially for heteroleptic systems prone to kinetic traps and component scrambling. Here, we report a guest-coupled reassembly strategy that enables programmable redistribution between cage architectures in heteroleptic pentagonal prismatic ZnII cages, assembled via precise edge-length matching between pentatopic and tetratopic ligands. Distinct from conventional single-guest templation, these cages exhibit adaptive redistribution behavior in which multiguest recognition is coupled to host redistribution within confined cavities. Chlorinated guests are selectively encapsulated through Cl···π and π···π interactions, thereby biasing the thermodynamic landscape of assembly. Secondary guests redirect the assembly equilibrium toward distinct product distributions, including guest release, guest exchange, or stoichiometry-dependent formation of species assigned as a homoleptic pseudo-cubic cage with one or two encapsulated guests. Crystallographic, Hirshfeld surface, and computational analyses reveal that multiple Cl···π, π···π, and C–H···π noncovalent interactions within the confined cavity contribute to the selectivity of guest-directed assembly redistribution. Furthermore, the incorporation of peripheral pyrene units imparts the prismatic cages with photoluminescence, which is enhanced upon guest binding due to framework rigidification. This work demonstrates how confined multiguest recognition can be coupled to compositional redistribution within complex heteroleptic assemblies, providing a foundation for programmable adaptive supramolecular systems.

title: Selective Hydrogen Transport Through Polymeric Fullerene Nanosheet Membranes
abstract: ABSTRACT Lamellar membranes, assembled from two‐dimensional (2D) nanosheets, have attracted intensive attention for molecular and ion sieving due to their tunable interlayer channels and ultrathin selective layers. However, molecular transport in conventional lamellar membranes usually occurs through interlayer galleries whose dimensions vary with stacking, limiting ångström‐scale control over selectivity. Therefore, developing a novel lamellar membrane with ångström‐scale in‐plane pores is highly desirable. In an idealized qTP lattice, four‐directionally connected fullerene cages define periodically distributed apertures that converge from an approximately 5.87 Å entrance to a 3.11 Å waist. Upon assembly, the constriction regions can discriminate by size, while their converging entrances and the intersheet galleries govern molecular access and transport resistance through the in‐plane apertures. The resulting polymeric fullerene nanosheet membrane exhibits an H 2 permeance of 3896 ± 107 GPU and an H 2 /CO 2 separation factor of 88.5 ± 5.9 for the separation of an equimolar H 2 /CO 2 mixture at 303.15 K and a total feed pressure of 100 kPa. The separation performance remains stable over 200 h of operation. This study establishes topology‐encoded pore geometry as a design principle for integrating short selective pathways with ångström‐scale molecular discrimination in lamellar membranes.

title: Engineering Synergistic Sites in a Cerium-Based Metal–Organic Framework for Photocatalytic CO2 Reduction
abstract: Abstract Photoreduction of CO2 to produce solar fuels is an important target. Redox-active Ce-based metal–organic frameworks (MOFs) are promising catalysts. Herein, we have synthesized an amino-functionalized Ce-based MOF, PKU-167 (PKU = Peking University). Upon introduction of Co(bpy)2Cl2 (bpy = 2,2′-bipyridine) to the skeleton of PKU-167, PKU-167-0.9Co achieved a high CO production rate of 18.4 mmol g–1 h–1 with a selectivity of 91.8% under visible-light irradiation and an apparent quantum yield of 1.97% at 425 nm. In situ characterizations and modeling reveal a synergistic adsorption–reduction mechanism, where amino groups enrich adsorption of CO2 for subsequent photoreduction on {Ce6} clusters and Co2+ sites in concert to achieve the optimal photocatalytic performance. This study will advance the rational design of redox-active Ce-based MOFs as efficient photocatalysts.

title: Quantum Sensing of Lithium Ions with Defect-Engineered Recognition Pockets in a TEMPO-Modified Covalent Organic Framework
abstract: Abstract Nuclear-spin quantum sensing requires coherent molecular electron spin qubits embedded in analyte-recognizing local environments that bring target nuclei into their short-range hyperfine detection volume. Here, we introduce TA-TEMPO, a covalent organic framework in which dilute nitroxide radicals and Li+-binding triazine moieties form defect-engineered recognition pockets for room-temperature 7Li sensing. Optimizing radical density preserves spin coherence while maximizing the 7Li/1H response acquired by hyperfine spectroscopy. TA-TEMPO detects Li+ in a tetrahydrofuran solution of LiBr with a sensitivity of 1.0 × 10–4 mol·L–1 at room temperature, a 50-fold improvement over the previous benchmark, and enables quantum sensing across several lithium-based electrolytes. Control experiments and density functional theory calculations show that triazine sites preferentially bind Li+ over Na+ and position it near nitroxide radicals, accounting for selective detection in a large excess of Na+. These results establish chemically programmed host–guest recognition as a strategy to integrate sensitivity, selectivity, and coherent spin readout in porous molecular quantum sensors.

title: Early Pathway Selection Precedes Conformational Locking in Protein Self-Assembly
abstract: Abstract When early intermediates begin to bias subsequent pathways during protein self-assembly remains difficult to resolve experimentally because early-stage processes are transient and poorly accessible. Here, using regenerated silk fibroin as a model system, we experimentally capture and analyze an early nucleation window in which assembly pathways begin to diverge before conformational locking occurs. By combining controlled electric-field perturbation with multiscale structural characterization and coarse-grained simulations, we identify reproducible nanoscale intermediates that mediate pathway selection. Within this window, electric fields bias early assembly kinetics in a nonmonotonic manner, modulating the formation, elongation, and competition of intermediates rather than directly enforcing structure or orientation. Time-resolved measurements show that subsequent growth proceeds primarily through elongation and fusion of existing intermediates, while β-sheet formation and crystallization emerge only at later stages and serve to stabilize pathways that were biased at earlier stages. Together, we locate the emergence of detectable pathway biasing within the nucleation stage and provide a framework for understanding and guiding protein self-assembly under nonequilibrium conditions.

title: Topology-Directed Pore Space Compartmentalization and Densification in MOFs Enable Record Trace C3H6 Capture and C2H4 Purification
abstract: Abstract Adsorptive separation of C3H6 from C2H4 is of great relevance yet highly challenging to the petrochemical industry, especially for trace C3H6 capture. Here, we constructed two metal–organic frameworks (MOFs), NKU-410 and NKU-411, through pillaring of the kgd- and hxl-topology supermolecular building layers (SBLs) comprised of a novel fluoride-bridging hexanuclear niccolite cluster. In terms of topological net merging and pillaring, a three-dimensional compartmentalization of pore space was implemented, reconstructing the less confined pore space in NKU-410 into a dense array of uniform strongly confined pore cavities in NKU-411. Leveraging the pore confinement effect, NKU-411 impressively attains an ultrahigh C3H6 uptake of 47.5 cm3 g–1 at 298 K and 0.01 bar, together with an appreciable C3H6/C2H4 (1/99, v/v) selectivity of 36.9, placing it among the benchmark MOFs for trace C3H6 capture from C2H4. Dynamic breakthrough experiments demonstrated that NKU-411 shows excellent C2H4 purification and C3H6 recovery performances at ambient conditions over a wide range of separation scenarios with varying feed concentrations and compositions, remarkably affording a record-breaking C2H4 (≥99.999% pure) productivity of 639.4 L kg–1 from C3H6/C2H4 (1/99, v/v) mixture. In-depth mechanistic studies disclosed that the well-tailored pore cavity in NKU-411 represents a “sweet spot” for C3H6 and the dense arrangement of such “sweet spot” maximally optimizes the pore space utilization, providing a new paradigm for boosting the ultralow-pressure gas adsorption capacity and selectivity for MOFs.

title: Diffusion-Gating Enabled Ternary C2H4 Purification and Inverse C2H2/CO2 Separation in an Adaptive Hopf-Link Metal–Organic Framework
abstract: Abstract The simultaneous purification of polymer-grade ethylene (C2H4) and recovery of high-purity acetylene (C2H2) from complex ternary mixtures with carbon dioxide (CO2) represents a critical industrial challenge. Conventional adsorbents employ thermodynamic selectivity to bind C2H2 and CO2 preferentially over C2H4, enabling one-step C2H4 purification but necessitating an energy-intensive desorption step for C2H2 recovery, as C2H2 typically binds more strongly. Here, we report a fundamentally different approach using diffusion-gating in an adaptive Hopf-link metal–organic framework, ZJNU-600, which replaces thermodynamic control. The framework comprises two orthogonal, interpenetrated sql nets mechanically interlocked as Hopf links, with thiocyanate linkers acting as molecular hinges that modulate the pore aperture. This architecture establishes an ideal kinetic diffusion hierarchy of CO2 &gt; C2H2 &gt; C2H4, completely inverting the elution order compared to equilibrium-based separation. Dynamic breakthrough experiments demonstrate that ZJNU-600 achieves one-step production of C2H4 from ternary mixtures while simultaneously enabling the direct recovery of C2H2 via inverse separation, eliminating the need for energy-intensive desorption. The exceptionally low isosteric heat of CO2 adsorption (24.7 kJ mol–1) further suggests minimal regeneration energy. Computational studies reveal that the diffusion barrier hierarchy arises from the differential chemical compatibility of each gas with the hydroxyl-decorated pore walls. This work establishes kinetic pore-aperture engineering as a generalizable and energy-efficient design principle for multicomponent gas separations, effectively inverting the separation hierarchy dictated by thermodynamic affinity.

title: Carbonyl‐Rich Polyimide Covalent Organic Frameworks as Anode Coating for Uniform Sodium Deposition
abstract: ABSTRACT Two‐dimensional covalent organic frameworks (2D COFs), by virtue of their structural diversity, high specific surface area, and facile functionalization, have emerged as a promising anode coating for sodium metal batteries (SMBs). Herein, we report two polyimide COFs (TATT‐NTCDA‑COF and TATT‐PMDA‑COF) constructed from isocyanurate‐based amine building blocks, which feature profuse ion‐binding active sites and a robust, ordered framework, thereby significantly enhancing ion transport, fostering uniform sodium deposition, and suppressing dendrite growth. Benefiting from this unique design and its reliable stability, the symmetric cell based on TATT‐NTCDA‑COF operates stably for over 1200 h at 0.1 mA cm −2 . When assembled into a full cell with a commercial Na 3 V 2 (PO 4 ) 3 (NVP) cathode, it delivers an initial discharge capacity of 107.4 mAh g −1 , retains 9.3% capacity after 800 cycles at 1 C, and maintains over 90% capacity retention even after 1390 cycles at 5 C and 750 cycles at 10 C. Thus, the rational design of carbonyl‐rich 2D COFs is of great significance for the construction of artificial anode coatings for SMBs.

title: Guest-Assisted Assembled Hydrogen-Bonded Organic Frameworks of Dysprosium Single-Ion Magnets
abstract: Abstract Lanthanide single-ion magnets (Ln-SIMs) have gradually emerged as one of the important candidates for next-generation magnetic materials. However, improving the environmental stability of Ln-SIMs remains one of the key challenges. Herein, we present a strategy for preparing highly thermostable Ln-SIMs through guest-assisted assembly of Ln-SIM-based hydrogen bonded organic frameworks (HOFs). Two HOFs based on Ln-SIMs, [HGdn]2[Dy(dpa)2(Hdpa)]·0.5Gdn·H2O (HOF-1) and [Dy(Hdpa)3]2·3H2O (HOF-2), have been prepared, where Gdn and H2dpa represent guanidine and pyridine-2,6-dicarboxylic acid, respectively. HOF-1 is constructed from [Dy(dpa)2(Hdpa)]2- anions and [HGdn]+ cations, giving rise to a three-dimensional HOF structure. HOF-2 consists of [Dy(Hdpa)3] units linked by guest H2O molecules to form a two-dimensional HOF. Both HOF-1 and HOF-2 exhibit excellent thermal stability. They can maintain their frameworks above 290 °C and thus rank among the most thermally stable Ln-SIMs reported to date. They also exhibit field-induced dual magnetic relaxation behaviors, with the highest effective energy barriers (Ueff) of 61.4 K (HOF-1) and 61.5 K (HOF-2), respectively. This work presents a novel approach for enhancing the structural stability of Ln-SIMs and regulating their magnetic properties through a guest-assisted assembly strategy for supramolecular HOF structures.

title: Intracellular Polymerization-Induced Self-Assembly of Peptide Nanosheets for Inflammatory Breast Cancer Therapy
abstract: Abstract Inflammatory breast cancer (IBC) is a highly aggressive breast cancer subtype characterized by diffuse, biologically invasive growth and poorly defined tissue boundaries, resulting in a high mortality rate even after multimodal treatment. Here, we report an intracellular polymerization-induced self-assembly (PISA) strategy that constructs mechanically active peptide nanosheets. Upon 365 nm UV irradiation, the photoinitiator Irgacure 2959 (I2959) initiates intracellular PISA of HisMAm in IBC cells. The corresponding nanosheets prepared in vitro exhibit a thickness of ∼30 nm and a wet-state apparent Young’s modulus of 8.02 ± 0.43 MPa. These nanosheets act through two coordinated materials-cell interactions: (i) increasing cellular viscosity and spatially associating with the actin cytoskeleton, suppressing cell migration and invasion; and (ii) accumulating in the endoplasmic reticulum and eliciting paraptosis-like cell death. In a subcutaneous IBC xenograft model, localized fiber-assisted light activation achieves 72.2% tumor growth inhibition without overt systemic toxicity. Overall, this work establishes intracellular PISA as a spatiotemporally controlled materials strategy for localized IBC treatment.

title: Linkage-sparing Assembly of Single-crystalline Phenylene-linked Covalent Organic Frameworks
abstract: Crystallising two-dimensional (2D) covalent organic frameworks (COFs) from irreversible bonds is hindered by the absence of error correction and out-of-plane disorder. Here, we establish linkage-sparing assembly (LSA) as a novel strategy for overcoming this limitation: preformed oligomeric motifs encode part of the target lattice, reducing the number of new irreversible C–C bonds required for framework growth. Combined with kinetic control through temperature and water content, LSA yields micrometre-scale single crystals of a phenylene-linked COF (HPPCOF) formed by ketone cyclotrimerisation. Electron diffraction resolves its honeycomb (hcb) structure and reveals local disorder and unreacted defects, providing insight into the real structure of an irreversibly formed 2D network. The heteroatom-free polyphenylene COF photocatalyses oxygen reduction to H2O2 via the oxygen reduction reaction, with activity comparable to heteroatom-containing COFs and without sacrificial electron donors. These results identify preassembly and kinetic control as complementary tools for crystallising robust COFs and broaden design opportunities for irreversible linkages.

title: LinkerGen: Guided Autoregressive Generation of Organic Linkers for Reticular Chemistry
abstract: Organic linker design for reticular materials requires balancing molecular diversity with structural and chemical constraints. Here, we introduce LinkerGen, a compact SMILES-based autoregressive model guided by chemical building unit (CBU) types, numerical property targets, or text descriptions. We train and evaluate two model sizes on approximately 22 million fragment-enumerated carboxylate linkers spanning 2-linear, 2-bent, and 3-planar CBU types. Model size and sampling temperature adjust the balance between validity and novelty, while conditioning increases the yield of distinct, valid, novel candidates satisfying selected requests compared with unconditioned generation followed by filtering. Text conditioning combines molecular requirements in a single natural-language request, although its effectiveness depends on training coverage and prompt formulation. A prospective application connects literature-informed linker generation to metal–organic polyhedron (MOP) assembly and calculated binding energies for 5-fluorouracil, illustrating how chemical design hypotheses can be explored through computational screening. LinkerGen provides a steerable source of candidate building units and a basis for adaptation to other linker families and design objectives through suitable training data and conditioning information. Highlights • Generative model for reticular organic chemical building units (CBUs) widen the chemical linker space available for the design of metal-organic polyhedra. • Conditioning enriches generated populations in linkers with desired properties. • Text conditioning allows complex chemical requirements to be effectively expressed in natural language.

title: Porphyrin Integration Enhances Bipolar Redox Accessibility for High‐Rate Sodium‐Based Dual‐Ion Storage
abstract: ABSTRACT Closing the gap between theoretical multielectron capacity and practical accessibility remains the central bottleneck for high‐energy organic batteries. Herein, we report a molecular design strategy that integrates a porphyrin motif into a sulfur‐rich conjugated polymer (BTTP) to align electronic structure, state‐dependent ion interactions, and electrochemical kinetics across the bipolar window. Despite possessing a lower theoretical capacity than its reference counterpart (BTB), BTTP achieves an exceptional theoretical capacity utilization of 94.2% (delivering 477 mAh g −1 at 0.5 A g −1 , compared to only 53.5% and 351 mAh g −1 for BTB). Electrokinetic analyses, including GITT and DRT, confirm accelerated apparent ion diffusion and reduced polarization limitations, enabling BTTP to retain 166 mAh g −1 at an ultrahigh current density of 20 A g −1 over 25 000 cycles. Operando/ex situ spectroscopy and theoretical calculations elucidate that the dual pyrrolic/imino nitrogen sites in porphyrin and the sulfur‐rich backbone cooperatively provide potential‐dependent coordination environments for PF 6 − anions and Na + cations. This work suggests that molecular regulation of complementary ion‐interaction environments within multi‐active‐unit frameworks, rather than simply increasing the number of redox units, is important for enhancing rate capability and capacity utilization.

title: PASS‐Derived O/S Donor Field‐Directed Competitive–Cooperative Fe/Co Phase Evolution for Cross‐Band Microwave Absorption
abstract: ABSTRACT Fe/Co bimetallic regulation enables high‐performance microwave absorbers, yet the role of intrinsic coordination disparity in precursor conversion, nonequilibrium phase evolution, and cross‐band loss redistribution remains unclear. We design a poly(arylene sulfide sulfone) (PASS)‐predefined O/S heterogeneous donor‐field strategy to direct competitive–cooperative nonequilibrium phase evolution in Fe/Co systems. Covalently embedded sulfone‐O and thioether‐S sites, with PASS's rigid backbone, create a molecularly preorganized donor field that amplifies non‐equivalent Fe/Co coordination, promoting competitive bonding, differentiated phase pathways, and electronic‐state reconstruction during confined pyrolysis. Fe/Co regulation thus reshapes local phases, O/S chemical environments, and interfacial charge states via Fe─O/Co─S coordination preferences, generating multiphase heterostructures, amorphous/crystalline interfaces, defects, and lattice strain while balancing dielectric polarization, conductive transport, magnetic response, and impedance matching. The resulting CFC absorber achieves cross‐band absorption in low‐frequency 5G and high‐frequency radar bands. CFC‐4 exhibits −73.83 dB at 6.23 GHz (3.20 mm) and −76.59 dB at 16.98 GHz (1.31 mm), with a maximum EAB of 5.03 GHz. CFC‐4∼6 (1–5 mm) show >90% cumulative effective absorption over 2–18 GHz. Finite‐element simulations reveal a maximum RCS reduction of 42.5 dB on PEC. This work establishes O/S donor‐field engineering as a viable route to amplify Fe/Co coordination differentiation for efficient cross‐band microwave absorption.

title: Sulfur Locking and Chlorination Synergistically Enable Efficient Charge Transport and Low Nonradiative Energy Loss in Organic Solar Cells
abstract: ABSTRACT Achieving efficient charge transport while maintaining low nonradiative energy loss remains a key challenge in the molecular design of small‐molecule acceptors (SMAs) for organic solar cells (OSCs). Herein, we report a stepwise molecular engineering strategy based on sulfur locking and chlorination to regulate intermolecular packing and excited‐state properties simultaneously. Sulfur locking modifies molecular conformation and intermolecular packing, leading to enhanced exciton diffusion and charge transport. Subsequent chlorination further strengthens intermolecular interactions through additional Cl···S contacts, resulting in tighter π–π stacking and improved crystalline ordering. Binary OSCs based on D18:Qx2Ph‐SCl achieve an efficiency of 20.0% with a high open‐circuit voltage ( V OC ) of 0.951 V, while maintaining a low nonradiative energy loss of ∼0.19 eV. Owing to its intrinsically lower reorganization energy and weaker electron–phonon coupling than L8‐BO, Qx2Ph‐SCl further serves as an effective third component in ternary OSCs, reducing nonradiative recombination and increasing the V OC . As a result, the ternary device delivers an efficiency of 21.3%. This work demonstrates that stepwise sulfur locking and chlorination provide an effective molecular design strategy for simultaneously optimizing charge transport and voltage loss in high‐performance OSCs.

title: Organocatalytic Enantiodifferentiation of Two Aryl Groups with Similar Steric Hindrances: Construction of gem ‐Diaryl Acyclic Quaternary Stereocenters
abstract: ABSTRACT Enantiodifferentiation of two aryl groups with similar steric hindrances is challenging. Although reactions involving diaryl ketones, diaryl alkenes, diaryl imines, diaryl carbenes, and diaryl radicals as substrates or intermediates have been reported for this purpose, successful enantiodifferentiation via diaryl conjugated carbanion intermediates has yet to be achieved. Moreover, existing methodologies predominantly rely on transition‐metal catalysis and are largely limited to the construction of gem ‐diaryl tertiary stereocenters, with no examples reported for the construction of gem ‐diaryl acyclic quaternary stereocenters. In this study, we have developed a phase‐transfer catalyst enabled enantiodifferentiation of two aryl groups with similar steric hindrances via diaryl conjugated carbanion intermediates. With this new approach, a variety of gem ‐diaryl compounds bearing acyclic all‐carbon quaternary stereocenters were synthesized in high yields and excellent enantioselectivities.

title: Stepwise Fusion Kinetics in Block Copolymer Micelles: Effect of Solvent Quality for the Corona
abstract: Abstract Block copolymer micelles in the strongly segregated regime are often trapped in nonequilibrium states, with large barriers to re-arrangement. Here, we show that micelle fusion can be induced, and its onset tuned, by controlling the solvent quality for the corona block. Small, kinetically trapped polystyrene-block-poly(ethylene oxide) (PS-PEO) micelles were prepared in two ionic liquids ([C4mim][BF4] and [C6mim][BF4]) and their mixtures, in which the PEO corona exhibits lower critical solution temperature phase behavior. Upon heating, synchrotron small-angle X-ray scattering and static light scattering reveal that the micelles grow irreversibly in discrete steps, as the second virial coefficient for PEO in the solvent approaches zero and even changes sign. The characteristic step temperatures vary linearly with the solvent composition, demonstrating that the onset of fusion is dictated by the corona–solvent interaction. A second-order kinetic model with an Arrhenius rate constant quantitatively describes the first fusion step and yields a large apparent activation energy of ca. 185 kJ/mol, independent of solvent composition. These results establish solvent quality for the corona as a key parameter regulating the fusion of kinetically trapped micelles and provide a general strategy for directing block copolymer assemblies toward equilibrium.

title: Supramolecular Assembly‐Driven Photofluorochromism Enables Time‐Encoded Transient Encryption
abstract: ABSTRACT Stimuli‐responsive luminescent materials offer dynamic optical outputs for advanced information security, yet achieving programmable fluorescence color evolution in water using a single optical input remains challenging. We developed a water‐soluble zwitterionic monomer, 2‐(pent‐4‐en‐1‐yl)isoquinolin‐2‐ium‐5‐sulfonate (IQIS), that exhibits pronounced photofluorochromism under ultraviolet (UV) irradiation. Its fluorescence evolves from blue to green, accompanied by an increase in the overall fluorescence quantum yield from 3.5% to 17.3%. Mechanistic studies reveal that IQIS is weakly pre‐associated in water, while UV irradiation promotes the growth, densification, and packing reorganization of these loose molecular clusters. The resulting long‐wavelength emission exhibits distinct aggregation‐dependent photophysical characteristics and is consistent with an aggregate‐associated excited state with enhanced intermolecular charge‐transfer character. By programming the kinetics of this supramolecular reorganization in different polymeric architectures, high‐resolution grayscale patterns with time‐evolving optical outputs can be generated. Under continuous UV irradiation, the same light used for fluorescence readout simultaneously drives the optical evolution, causing initially visible information to progressively fade and ultimately disappear without an additional stimulus. This single‐input, self‐evolving behavior enables a “Snapchat‐like” transient encryption mode and provides a strategy for spatiotemporal information encoding based on kinetically programmed supramolecular photofluorochromism.

title: Particle-Mediated Tuning of Defect Stability in Lamellar Block Copolymer Systems
abstract: Abstract We study how colloidal inclusions modify the formation energy of dislocation pairs in lamellar block copolymer systems. Using a hybrid particle/Ginzburg–Landau model, we calculate defect formation energies by comparing defect-free and defect-containing states with and without embedded colloids. Finite-size scaling is used to obtain formation energies in the thermodynamic limit. The effect of colloid insertion depends strongly on particle sizes and surface patterning. Homogeneous particles increasingly stabilize dislocation pairs with increasing particle sizes. Particles larger than one lamellar domain preferentially occupy the dislocation cores, where they replace strained polymer rather than deforming defect-free lamellae. The magnitude of this stabilization depends on surface affinity. Balanced Janus particles instead increase the formation energy, because their competing surface preferences cannot be satisfied simultaneously near the curved core. Varying the patch ratio interpolates between these limits. Surface patterning has little effect for particles smaller than one lamellar domain, but changes the formation energy by several tens of reduced energy units (roughly 10–40 kBT for typical block copolymers) for larger particles. These results provide quantitative guidelines for controlling topological defect stability in lamellar block copolymer systems.

title: ATP-dependent dimerization of BrxC coordinates BrxBCZ assembly for phage exclusion
abstract: Abstract Bacteriophage Exclusion (BREX) systems protect bacterial genomes via sequence-specific DNA methylation while blocking phage replication through a poorly understood “restriction-without-cleavage” mechanism. Here, we present cryo-EM structures and functional characterization of the core BREX machinery from Escherichia coli . We determined the structures of the ATPase BrxC in its monomeric state and two ATPγS-bound dimeric conformations, showing that ATP binding, not hydrolysis, triggers dimerization. The conserved Arg328 couples dimer formation to ATP hydrolysis and is required for both phage restriction and host methylation; the R328A mutant supports assembly but abolishes defense. We further resolved the BrxBCZ ternary complex, revealing BrxB as a central scaffold bridging the BrxC dimer and BrxZ without direct BrxC–BrxZ contact. Biochemical assays show that BrxZ is a dual-function enzyme with alkaline phosphatase and metal-dependent nuclease activities. Thus, ATP drives BrxC assembly and inhibits BrxZ activities. Disruption of the BrxB–BrxC interface or the BrxC ATPase cycle selectively eliminates restriction while preserving methylation, establishing BrxBCZ as a restriction-specific structural core. Collectively, these findings delineate the structural basis for ATP-dependent coordination of BREX, revealing how energy metabolism is integrated into bacterial innate immunity.

title: Mixed Thiolate/Alkoxide Antimony Cages for Reversed-Bilayer Vesicle Self-Assembly and Dye Protection in Organic Media
abstract: A new two-step synthesis produces moisture-stable antimony and arsenic dithiothreitol cages. Structural analysis reveals that the Sb compounds self-assemble into reversed bilayers, consistent with pnictogen-bonded vesicle formation in organic media. The Sb assemblies more efficiently encapsulate and protect rhodamine B than the arsenic analogue or a topological mimic that lacks pnictogen-bonding capability. This work provides a synthetically accessible tool for partitioning organic media to allow for orthogonal reactivity.

title: Water Rolls Off, Current Flows: The Rise of Conductive Superhydrophobic Textiles
abstract: ABSTRACT Conductive superhydrophobic textiles uniquely combine electrical conductivity with extreme water repellency, enabling humidity‐resistant wearable electronics, smart protective clothing, and self‐powered systems. This review systematically examines the design principles, fabrication strategies, and multifunctional applications of these materials, with a focus on the core interfacial coupling mechanism—water rolls off, current flows—that governs their performance. Key application domains are critically analyzed, with emphasis on how superhydrophobic protection enhances device stability under humid, sweaty, or rainy conditions. The review identifies fundamental bottlenecks—conductive network failure under deformation, poor durability of hydrophobic interfaces, and inherent trade‐offs between conductivity and water repellency—that currently limit practical deployment. A structured translation roadmap from laboratory design to scalable manufacturing is presented, incorporating the development workflow of discovery, design, fabrication, testing, validation, qualification, scaling, deployment, impact, and sustainability. Future directions, including stretchable self‐healing architectures, artificial intelligence (AI)‐guided inverse design, fluorine‐free sustainable manufacturing, and self‐powered wireless textile systems, are discussed with technical specificity. This review provides a unified framework connecting materials chemistry, textile engineering, and device physics, guiding researchers and engineers toward transforming these materials from laboratory prototypes to real‐world products that enhance human safety, comfort, and connectivity.

title: Covalent Organic Pillars: Programmable Nanotubular Cavitands
abstract: Conspectus For more than half a century, the construction of molecular host compounds has emerged as a central theme in supramolecular chemistry, driven by the promise of controlling molecular recognition, transport, and reactivity. While a wide variety of macrocyclic hosts have been developed, achieving deep-cavity cavitands with confined inner spaces extending over several nanometers has remained challenging. This limitation has hindered systematic investigations of how confinement governs molecular behavior within the so-called “inner phase”, as originally articulated by Cram. Motivated by these challenges, our laboratory has pursued the design and synthesis of a family of covalent organic pillars (COPs)─single-molecule nanotubular architectures assembled through dynamic covalent imine condensation of aldehyde-functionalized paracyclophane building blocks with diamine linkers. In this Account, we summarize our efforts to establish COPs as a versatile class of open-ended nanotubular cavitands, offering highly preorganized one-dimensional cavities with lengths exceeding 2 nm that encapsulate guests with complementary size and surface properties. By adopting an isoreticular design strategy, we demonstrate that systematic variation of linker structure and length enables the construction of a series of COPs with precisely tunable cavity length, sidewall composition, and effective channel width. This modularity provides a rare opportunity to correlate host geometry with recognition behavior in a quantitative and predictive manner. Beyond host–guest chemistry, we show that COPs also provide a powerful platform for exploring dynamic stereochemical phenomena during self-assembly from inherently chiral yet stereolabile macrocyclic building blocks. Whereas COPs constructed from rigid diamine spacers undergo exclusive narcissistic chiral self-sorting, yielding pairs of enantiomeric nanotubular structures, incorporation of flexible aliphatic diamine spacers leads to pronounced odd–even effects in chiral self-sorting, giving either racemic mixtures of chiral COPs or achiral meso-COPs, depending on linker parity. This conformational flexibility further endows COPs with adaptive host–guest recognition behavior, enabling cooperative accommodation of guests through a balance of host deformation and guest distortion. A distinctive feature of our work is that the molecular structures of essentially all COPs and their key host–guest complexes are elucidated by single-crystal X-ray crystallography, providing a rigorous structural foundation that remains rare for deep-cavity molecular hosts. Overall, our studies establish COPs as a precision design paradigm for nanotubular cavitands that bridge the gap between discrete macrocycles and extended porous frameworks, thereby opening a new regime of molecular control in supramolecular chemistry.

title: Advances on triply periodic hyperbolic surface structures: from biological inspiration to artificial self-assembly
abstract: Triply periodic hyperbolic surfaces (TPHSs) are a class of complex structures that extend periodically throughout three-dimensional space and possess smooth surfaces with non-positive Gaussian curvature. They appear in a wide range of natural systems, from cellular membranes to butterfly wing scales and beetle exoskeletons. Owing to their unique geometries and extraordinary properties, TPHSs have attracted extensive attention and research interest. Detailed structural characterizations of naturally occurring TPHSs have been performed, and a variety of artificial analogs have been fabricated by top-down physical methods and bottom-up chemical approaches. These efforts have deepened our understanding of TPHSs and broadened their application scope. This review discusses the progress on TPHSs in biological systems and their artificial synthesis, and it surveys current applications of these structures in fields such as photonics, energy storage and conversion, catalysis, sensing, thermal management and mechanical metamaterials. It thereby provides a new framework linking biological structures to artificial structures. Finally, this review concludes by outlining current challenges and proposing directions for future research.

title: Macroscopic two-dimensional sheets by chemically triggered self-assembly.
abstract: Bottom-up self-assembly of two-dimensional (2D) sheets is rare. We present in situ reaction driven self-assembly for semithroughput synthesis of imine based 2D materials. Easily tuneable molecular structures and reaction kinetics allow for up to seven sheet forming systems.

title: Recent Advances in the Photocatalytic Reduction of Hexavalent Chromium Using Mesoporous Materials: A Review
abstract: The hazards associated with hexavalent chromium, Cr(VI), have prompted extensive research into treatment technologies for chromium-containing industrial effluents. Selection of an appropriate process depends on wastewater composition, treatment objectives, cost-effectiveness, operational feasibility, and monitoring and maintenance requirements. Mesoporous materials, with pore diameters of 2–50 nm, offer accessible surfaces and pore networks that can support adsorption and photocatalytic reactions. Following the independent discovery of ordered mesoporous materials in the early 1990s by researchers at Mobil and other research groups, their tunable physicochemical properties have supported applications across environmental catalysis. In Cr(VI) photoreduction, accessible surface area, pore connectivity, and surface functionality influence chromium-oxyanion adsorption and reactant transport, while semiconductor composition and interfacial architecture govern light absorption and charge-carrier behaviour. This review examines recent advances in mesoporous photocatalysts for Cr(VI) reduction, focusing on the relationships between pore structure, chemical composition, and reported treatment performance. Metal oxides, carbon-based composites, metal–organic and covalent organic frameworks, and heterostructured systems are discussed alongside strategies involving doping, sensitisation, and interfacial engineering. Particular attention is given to distinguishing adsorption and direct photolysis from photocatalytic reduction and to interpreting performance under different irradiation, pH, and electron-donor conditions. The reviewed literature indicates that mesostructuring can enhance photoreduction when accessible pores are combined with suitable surface chemistry and efficient charge utilisation. However, differences in experimental conditions limit direct comparison between materials. Catalyst recovery, aqueous stability, metal leaching, realistic wastewater matrices, and reactor design remain central considerations in translating laboratory performance into sustainable treatment applications.

title: Anionic Phase-Transfer Catalysis for Constructing Chiral Sulfur Centers via Asymmetric Sulfinimidation
abstract: Abstract Chiral anion phase-transfer (CAPT) catalysis has emerged as a powerful strategy for asymmetric catalysis, yet its stereocontrol modes remain largely limited to π-face differentiation or enantiotopic bond selection. The ability to exert stereocontrol through enantioselective recognition of heteroatom lone pairs remains underdeveloped, restricting catalytic access to configurationally stable heteroatom-centered stereocenters. Here, we report a CAPT platform that enables asymmetric sulfinimidation through enantioselective halogenation of prochiral sulfur(II) lone pairs, providing direct access to chiral aryl and alkyl sulfinimidate esters with high enantioselectivity. Mechanistic studies and computational investigations confirm that halogenation is the enantiodetermining step, forming a chiral, configurationally stable sulfinimidoyl fluoride intermediate. Enantioselective oxidation of prochiral sulfides indicates that this CAPT lone-pair recognition platform may be more generally applicable to heteroatom lone pairs. These findings establish lone-pair differentiation as a new mode of stereocontrol in CAPT and expand the conceptual scope of chiral anionic catalysis toward the asymmetric synthesis of chiral organosulfur compounds.
